speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I indicated to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) my intention to raise this point of order at the beginning of Proceedings today once I had the opportunity of seeing Hansard from yesterday which came late today as Your Honour will know.
I rise on the basis of exchanges yesterday between the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition. It is to be found at page 6391 of Hansard. I am sure you will be aware, Mr. Speaker, of Citation 321(3) of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition which states in part:
The Speaker has traditionally protected from attack a group of individuals commonly referred to as "those of high official station". The extent of this group has never been defined. Over the years it has covered senior public servants-
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition clearly made an attack on the integrity on the Governor of the Bank of Canada. He said in the House yesterday, and I quote:
The question really relates to the fact that the House was misled ... being misled by the ... Governor of the Bank of Canada.
The point of order which I wish to raise is a very serious one. An unsubstantiated accusation has been made by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, who is an officer of the House, Sir, which constitutes an attack on a senior public servant who, in discharging his responsibilities, gave advice to the Government.
When the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, who is an experienced Parliamentarian, engages in a partisan attack on a leading public administrator, our system is undermined. The Prime Minister can defend himself. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) can defend himself. The Governor of the Bank of Canada cannot.

Come on.
September 10, 1985

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: To say that the Governor misled the House is, I suggest, Sir, using the privileges of Parliament to protect oneself against an action which, very simply, if stated outside the House of Commons and outside of the protection of the House of Commons would be libelous in nature and subject to the commencement of legal proceedings, in my estimation.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: What a lawyer!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It has been the custom here for Hon. Members of this House, when they have uttered words which in effect constitute an attack upon a senior government official-with whom the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition has had personal contact in his ministerial capacity-to do the honourable thing; stand in their place and withdraw the offending words and apologize, in this case, to the Governor of the Bank of Canada. I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to find that there has been a breach in terms of Beauchesne and to ask the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition to withdraw his remarks and apologize to Mr. Bouey.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address the point of order raised by the House Leader. He did give me verbal notice of his intent to do this as the House began proceedings this afternoon. What I said was, and I quote:
The question really relates to the fact that the House was misled, including this side of the House, when we supported the Minister of Finance in the original bail-out Bill for that purpose. That is what it gets down to-the question of incompetence and the House being misled by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, and indeed, the Governor of the Bank of Canada.
Those are the words which are being challenged. Let me go to the technical point first. If one looks at Citation 320 in Beauchesne's Fifth Edition we find, in looking at the word "misled", that it has been consistently held by the House that it must be "deliberately misled".
I submit to Your Honour that if you go further to Citation 321, which relates to protected persons, that is to say not just Hon. Members of the House but those persons traditionally protected, you find they are a group of individuals commonly referred to as "those of high official station". I am not going to argue for the purposes of your ruling, Mr. Speaker, whether the Governor of the Bank of Canada is of high official station or not, but I will assume he is. I will concede that point. However, 1 submit to Your Honour that the same judgment you have to apply concerning misleading statements or unparliamentary language regarding Members of this House should also be applied against protected persons. In other words, I used the word "misled"; I did not use the words "deliberately misled". I also want to refer Your Honour to Citation 323(2) regarding unparliamentary language, which reads:
The proper time to raise such a point of order is when the words are used and not afterwards.
Even if there were a point of order, it is already too late. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) points out that it was
Point of Order-Mr. Hnatyshyn challenged by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) yesterday, but not on a point of order. I also refer Your Honour to Citation 324(2), which reads:
An expression which is deemed to be unparliamentary today does not necesari-ly have to be deemed unparliamentary next week.
Let us get down to the substance. -an agreement was reached this morning ... which will ensure the long-term viability of this Edmonton-based bank.

He goes further to ask me to consider questions of fact. I think he knows full well that I cannot do so even though, for his reasons, he may wish to put them in the record.
I must find, under the practices of the House, that whatever happened yesterday happened yesterday, and it happened yesterday.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, sovereignty can be a very emotional issue in this country, and that is quite understandable, since sovereignty involves the identity and the very character of a people. We Canadians want to be ourselves. We want to manage our own affairs and control our own destiny, but we also want to go beyond this to play a constructive role in a world that is become increasingly inter-dependent. We have something to offer and at the same time we have something to gain.
Since it came to power, this Government has shown a keen interest in the sovereignty issue. We have consolidated national unity, because a house divided cannot stand. We have reinforced the national economy, because sovereignty means nothing without solvency. Unity and strength: these are the hallmark of sovereignty and of the policies and achievements of this Government.

We have declared a Canadian ownership policy in respect of foreign investment in the publishing industry. We have made our own Canadian decisions on controversial issues of foreign policy, whether in Nicaragua or South Africa. We have passed the Foreign Extraterritorial Measures Act to block unacceptable claims of jurisdiction by foreign Governments or foreign courts seeking to extend their writ to Canada. We have arrested foreign trawlers poaching in our fishing zones. We have taken important steps to bolster and improve Canada's defences, notably in increasing Canadian forces in Europe and in putting into place a new North Warning System to protect Canadian sovereignty over our northern airspace.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As well, Sir, we have reconstructed relations with traditional friends and allies who have welcomed our renewed unity and strength and the confidence they generate.
Sir, my colleague, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse), and other Ministers of this Government on other occasions, will be making announcements through the life of this Parliament on other steps this Government intends to take to assert and guarantee the sovereignty and independence of Canada. In domestic policy, foreign policy, and defence policy the Government has given Canadian sovereignty a new impetus within a new maturity. However, Sir, much remains to be done. The voyage of the Polar Sea demonstrated that Canada, in the past, had not developed the means to ensure our sovereignty over time. During that voyage, Canada's legal position was fully protected, but when we looked for ways to
September 10, 1985

exercise our sovereignty we found that the Canadian cupboard was nearly bare. We obtained from the United States a formal and explicit assurance that the voyage of the Polar Sea was without prejudice to Canada's legal position. That, Sir, is an assurance which the Government of the day in 1969 did not receive for the voyage of the Manhattan and of the two United States Coast Guard ice breakers. Sir, whatever was done this summer, and however it may contrast with what was done before, nonprejudicial arrangements will not be enough in the future.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The voyage of the Polar Sea has left no trace on Canada's Arctic waters and no mark on Canada's Arctic sovereignty. It is behind us and our concern must be for what lies ahead. Many countries, including the United States and the Federal Republic of Germany, are actively preparing now for commercial navigation in Arctic waters. Developments are accelerating in ice science, ice technology, and in tanker design. Several major Japanese firms are moving to capture the market for ice breaking tankers once polar oil and gas come on stream. Soviet submarines are being deployed under the Arctic ice pack and the United States Navy has, in turn, identified a need to gain Arctic operational experience to counter new Soviet deployments.
The implications for Canada are clear. As the western country with by far the greatest frontage on the Arctic, we must come up to speed in a range of marine operations that bear on our capacity to exercise effective control over the Northwest Passage and our other Arctic waters. To this end, Sir, I wish to declare to the House the policy of the Government in respect of Canadian sovereignty in Arctic waters, and to make a number of announcements as to how we propose to give expression to that policy.
Canada is an Arctic nation. The international community has long recognized that the Arctic mainland and islands are a part of Canada like any other, but the Arctic is not only a part of Canada, it is a part of Canadian greatness. The policy of the Government is to preserve that Canadian greatness undiminished. Canada's sovereignty in the Arctic is indivisible. It embraces land, sea and ice. It extends without interruption to the seaward-facing coasts of the Arctic islands. These islands are joined, and not divided, by the waters between them. They are bridged for most of the year by ice. From time immemorial Canada's Inuit people have used and occupied the ice as they have used and occupied the land. The policy of the Government is to maintain the natural unity of the Canadian Arctic archipelago and to preserve Canada's sovereignty over land, sea and ice undiminished and undivided.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That Canadian sovereignty has long been upheld by Governments of this country. However, no previous Government has defined its precise limits or delineated Canada's internal waters and territorial sea in the Arctic.
Statements by Ministers
This Government proposes to do so. An Order in Council establishing straight baselines around the outer perimeter of the Canadian Arctic archipelago has been signed today and will come into effect on January 1, 1986.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
These baselines define the outer limit of Canada's historical internal waters. Canada's territorial waters extend 12 miles seaward off the baselines. While the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act requires 60 days notice only for the establishment of fishery limits, we consider prior notice should also be given for this important step of establishing straight baselines.

Canada's jurisdiction over its continental margin and 200-mile fishing zone is unchallenged in the Arctic as elsewhere. Canada also exercises jurisdiction over a 100-mile pollution prevention control zone in arctic waters, in order to protect the unique ecological balance in the area. That too has been recognized by the international community, in a special provision in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
However, no previous government had ever extended the application of Canadian civil and criminal laws to offshore zones in the Arctic and elsewhere. The present Government will take this action. To this end, one of our priorities will be the speedy passage of legislation covering the offshore application of Canada laws.
The exercise of functional jurisdiction in Arctic waters is essential to Canadian interests. However, it is no substitute for Canada's full sovereignty over the waters of the Arctic archipelago. Only with full sovereignty can we protect the entire range of Canadian interests. Full sovereignty is vital to Canada's security. It is vital to the Inuit people. And it is vital to Canada's national identity.
The policy of this Government is to exercise full sovereignty in and on the waters of the Arctic Archipelago and this applies to the airspace above as well. We will accept no substitute. [English]
The policy of the Government is also to encourage the development of the navigation in Canadian Arctic waters. Our goal is to make the Northwest Passage a reality for Canadians and foreign shipping as a Canadian waterway.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Navigation, however, will be subject to the controls and other measures required for Canada's security, for the preservation of the environment, and for the welfare of the Inuit and other inhabitants of the Canadian Arctic. In due course the Government will announce the further steps it is taking to implement these policies, and especially to provide more extensive marine support services, to strengthen regulatory structures, and to reinforce the necessary means of control. I am announcing today that the Government has decided to construct a Polar Class-8 ice-breaker.

September 10, 1985
Statements by Ministers
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My colleagues, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) will shortly bring to Cabinet recommendations with regard to the design and construction plans. The costs are very high, in the order of $.5 billion, but the Government is not about to conclude that Canada cannot afford the Arctic.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Meanwhile, we are taking immediate steps to increase surveillance overflights over Arctic waters by Canadian Forces aircraft. In addition, we are now making plans for naval activity in Eastern Arctic waters in 1986. Canada is a strong and responsible member of the international community. Our strength and our responsibility make us all the more aware of the need for co-operation with other countries, and especially with our friends and allies. Co-operation is necessary, not only in defence of our own interests, but in defence of the common interests of the international community. Co-operation adds to our strength and in no way diminishes our sovereignty. The policy of the Government is to offer its co-operation to its friends and allies and to seek their co-operation in return.
We are prepared to explore with the United States all means of co-operation that might promote the respective interests of both countries as Arctic friends, neighbours and allies in the Arctic waters of Canada and Alaska. The United States has been made aware that Canada wishes to open talks on this matter in the near future. Any co-operation with the United States or with other Arctic nations shall only be on the basis of full respect for Canada's sovereignty. That too has been made clear.
In 1970, the Government of the day barred the International Court of Justice from hearing disputes that might arise concerning the jurisdiction exercised by Canada for the prevention of pollution in Arctic waters. The Government of that day said to that court, "Your jurisdiction shall not affect Canada. We will not put our case before that court". This Government will remove that bar. Indeed, we have today notified the Secretary General of the United Nations that Canada is withdrawing the 1970 reservation to its acceptance of the compulsory jurisdiction of the World Court.
The Arctic is a heritage for the people of Canada. They are determined to keep their heritage entire and to keep their heritage intact. The policy of this Government is to give full expression to that determination.
We challenge no established rights, for none have been established except by Canada. We set no precedents for other areas, for no other area compares with the Canadian Arctic archipelago. We are confident in our position. We believe in the rule of law in international relations. We shall act in accordance with our confidence and belief, as we are doing
today in withdrawing the 1970 reservation to Canada's acceptance of the compulsory jurisdiction of the World Court. We are prepared to uphold our position in that Court, if necessary, and to have it fully and freely judged there.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, these are the measures we are announcing today: first, immediate adoption of an Order in Council establishing straight baselines around the Arctic archipelago, to be effective January 1, 1986; second, immediate adoption of a Canadian Laws Offshore Application Act; third, immediate talks with the United States on co-operation in Arctic waters on the basis of full respect for Canadian sovereignty; fourth, an immediate increase of surveillance overflights of our Arctic waters by aircraft of the Canadian Forces, and immediate planning for Canadian naval activity in the Eastern Arctic in 1986; fifth, the immediate withdrawal of the 1970 reservation to Canada's acceptance of the compulsory jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice; and sixth, construction of a polar, class 8 ice-breaker and urgent consideration of other means of exercising more effective control over our Arctic waters.
These are the measures which we can take immediately. We know, however, that a long-term commitment is required. We are making that commitment today.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to receive the Right Hon. Minister's statement. My only objection is that it is exactly three months too late. When I rose in the House in the middle of June to raise this issue, the Minister remained silent, and today he rose in the House to propose a series of measures that would have been unnecessary if the Government had been truly in control of the situation last summer, when the problem arose.

We have been hearing about the great friendship between the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) and President Reagan of the United States for many, many months. For 15 years the Americans have protested the Bill that I introduced in the House of Commons in 1970 concerning the prevention of Arctic pollution. For 15 years the Americans did not want to challenge the sovereignty of Canada which was reinforced at that time. They never sent a ship through our waters for 15 years.
In September, 1984, when my leader was Prime Minister, they did not come to challenge our sovereignty. They did not do so in the 14 previous years with former Prime Minister Trudeau. However, this summer, with their great friend, the Prime Minister of Canada in office they came and humiliated him. They also came and humiliated the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). Worse still, they came and humiliated the whole nation by challenging our sovereignty in the north.
If it is true that the motto of the two Governments today is "good frienship", it would have been so easy for the Prime
September 10, 1985

Minister to call President Reagan and simply explain our case. The first argument given by the Americans for the voyage was that it wanted to save $500,000. Imagine, the poor little Defence Department of the United States needing to save that money. We could have sent them a cheque for $500,000 and offered to pay the gas to go through the canal rather than challenge our sovereignty. However, the Government was silent. Now that the horses have left, it is attempting to close the gate.
It did the same thing yesterday. After appointing one Tory person every three hours since it came to power, suddenly it closes the gate on patronage appointments because the number of Tories needing jobs is decreasing. I hope the Minister recognizes what he is doing. There was a strategy behind what took place in the past with regard to our sovereignty because the key in international affairs was he exercising of jurisdiction and we have had that jurisdiction and we have exercised it. This began under Louis St. Laurent when we ensured for many years that there were RCMP, Armed Forces and viable Inuit villages in these areas in order to inform the world that it was Canadian land.
Time is a very important element. When sovereignty is exercised for 100 years, no one can challenge it. Today, the Minister is taking a gamble and making a bold move which might cause the court to look into this case. Now we will either win or lose. The Minister could have been prudent and carried on with our acts of sovereignty protection this summer, without anyone being able to challenge it. We could have used all the "supposed friendship" this government has in the world to make sure our sovereignty was not challenged. Our sovereignty would have been greater in 50 or 100 years.
I hope the Minister will not have to get up in the House in the future to say he is sorry but it is typical of how this Government reacts. It does not know where to go. It makes a decision and then backs off. Last summer my leader challenged the Government to call President Reagan. I raised this problem many times during the summer and I raised this question in the House of Commons. However, the Minister is too late again, fumbling and trying to repair the disaster and humiliation of the nation which his inaction has caused.
We will have to support that action now because we have no choice. He has opened the case in court. 1 hope we will win but I believe that 50 or 100 more years of sovereignty exercised by the Government, with no challenge from anyone, would have been better. If it is true that there is a policy of friendship with the Government of the United States, it is a shame that President Reagan sent a quasi military ship in our water this summer despite the requests and pleas of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. If we had a Prime Minister who did not always go to the President on his knees, we would have been in a position to challenge the President and say that we will not tolerate such action. We would not be put in the shameful position we are today.
Statements by Ministers
I hope in this case the Minister is sure of himself. 1 hope we will not lose. I wish the Minister well. He would have been well advised last summer, rather than to laugh at my question in the House of Commons, to have taken the problem seriously and acted.
Hear, hear!
We would have more positive results now. Probably it is now too late. If the Government wanted to act, why were these actions not proclaimed in July? It was not a technical problem.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Or last year.

Yes, or last year or 10 years ago. In court, it is not for the one who occupies land to provoke a case. At least I know that. When I have a good case I do not necessarily go to court myself. I wait for the other guy. You never know what the court's decision might be. When you own land, you do not go to court yourself. You wait until your ownership is challenged. That is basic law I learned at university.
Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, I fear it is too late. I pray to God that the Minister has not created a situation on which we will be prematurely challenged. I am sad today because the danger is now more than ever caused because we had a Government that did not know what to do. The Government was afraid to offend President Reagan. This Government let him challenge and humiliate Canadians. After the humiliation lasted all summer, the Government comes with an ice-breaker. I am not impressed with the ice-breaker. With the disaster of the Canadian Commercial Bank, we could build two more ice-breakers.
Hear, hear!
I just pray the Minister knows what he is doing. If he had not acted as as slowly on such an important matter, he does all the time, we would not be in the awful situation in which we are today.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I agree with one of the remarks of the previous speaker that Canadians were humiliated by the Polar Sea incident. The image many Canadians have of the new Conservative administration is that a green light has been given to the White House to use our Arctic as a military and economic playground. The image of our Arctic as the new battle-line of fortress America toward the Soviet Union is not without foundation.
Let me deal first with the matter of the Polar Sea. I have confirmed today with the Canadian Coastguard that not one but seven Canadian Coastguard ice-breakers could have gone through the passage ahead of the Polar Sea. This is a matter of marine sovereignty. The films of overflights from Canadian aircraft were interesting at best, but did little to express the Canadian mood on this issue or to achieve basic requirements
6466

September 10, 1985
Statements by Ministers
under international law. The Louis St. Laurent was available, the Sir John A. Macdonald was in the area and was available and, the John Cabot was available. Three R-class 1200s, the Des Groseillers, the Pierre Radisson, the Sir John Franklin and even the Norman McLeod Rogers were available. One of these vessels should have preceded the Polar Sea and the U.S. should have been billed every maple leaf penny of the cost. Only in Viscount Melville Sound did pack ice even slow down the Polar Sea, and throughout this so-called without prejudice journey, we should have followed our own precedent of 1969 when the Sir John A. Macdonald accompanied the Manhattan.
Hear, hear!

Parliament then moved quickly to enact the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Control Act just months after the penetration of our sovereignty by the Manhattan. Parliament then should have moved to designate closing line or straight baselines as they are known around the outer perimeter of the Arctic archipelago. I pay tribute to the Right Hon. Minister for putting in place today such law to become effective January 1, 1986.
By demarcating our headland to headland closing lines, we will demonstrate to the international community our internal waters, which was at issue with the Polar Sea, our 12 mile territorial sea, our 100 mile pollution prevention control zone, our 200 mile fishing zone, our 200 mile limit and our 200 mile and beyond continental margin. These are pressing and urgent matters of national sovereignty, and I look forward to seeing them in The Canada Gazette and on all international marine charts.
1 also pay tribute to the Minister for producing the Canadian Laws Offshore Application Act. I look forward to seeing it, although I accept the Minister's words that it fully extends the application of Canadian civil and criminal laws to offshore areas, the Arctic included.
In 1975, the Polar 10 was considered for construction here in Canada, a nuclear-powered class 10 ice-breaker. The Government did not proceed. Since 1977, the conceptualization and design of the 100,000 horsepower gas-diesel electrically-driven Polar 8 has been on the drawing board, some eight years now. Tenders will be complete by December, I am advised, and this vital new vessel to exert Canadian sovereignty will be under construction, we hope, in the new year. All Canadians should support this vital component of our Arctic sovereignty.
On our boundaries we have successfully negotiated agreements with Greenland in such areas as the Davis Strait and Baffin Bay. Now we must move on the Labrador Sea. By demarcating these boundaries headland to headland with Greenland, let us not forget the crying need to move on the 141st meridian with Alaska in the western Arctic, Dixon Entrance and our rights in the Gulf of Alaska as well as the Straits of Juan de Fuca off Vancouver. Previous administrations have been lax, and under former Prime Minister Trudeau
to the point of losing ground on some of these boundary issues with the United States.
Let us not forget that as recently as last summer during the election, the United States Secretary of the Interior had a piece of Canada for sale off the Queen Charlotte Islands for gas and oil development. It was only under pressure from my Party that steps were taken that resulted in the withdrawal of that sale.
On this point, I urge the Minister today to direct Petro-Canada under the Canada Oil and Gas Lands Act, Bill C-48, to register submarine rights to the maximum, to all our boundary positions as outlined by myself and the new declarations. This is vital as we so sadly learned concerning the Georges Bank case most recently before the World Court.
The Right Hon. Minister, like many of his predecessors, climbs on the backs of the Inuit and other aboriginal Canadians to plant Canada's flag. To be intellectually and constitutionally honest, the Government must now move forward promptly to deal with the matter of aboriginal title and rights thereto.
There are no legal treaties with our first citizens north of 60, despite our constitutional recognition and affirmation of their rights. Do not forget, Mr. Minister, that in 1953 and again in 1955 the Inuit were taken from their homes by the federal Government to Cornwallis and Ellesmere Island. On that point, as recently as yesterday, I received a letter from the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs (Mr. Crombie) indicating that he does not intend to move on that very important Inuit matter, particularly regarding the elders who want to move home from those two communities. They were transplanted to exert Canada's sovereignty. I urge the Minister will all sincerity to move now with this House to settle their title, which as the Minister says, has been outstanding since time immemorial, on the land, water and ice of the Arctic. Now is the time to act on this vital constitutional matter.
On the matters of the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zone Act, I trust the Minister intends to move forward quickly with notice on these new fisheries limits. I trust that he and his colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser), will ensure that these matters are referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
On the matter of notifying the Secretary General of the United Nations today of our intention to withdraw the 1970 reservation, to accept compulsory jurisdiction to the World Court regarding disputes that may arise concerning Canadian jurisdiction for the prevention of pollution in Arctic waters, 1 warn the Minister that there are steps he must now urgently take to set our house in order first, some of which I have touched upon. In particular, I advise the Minister to look with care at the matter of the MV Arctic. The Minister's colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) just this summer exempted that vessel by Order in Council from the strict requirements of the Arctic Waters Marine Prevention Control Act to carry crude oil south from Cameron Island, as part of Pan Arctic's Bent Horn project. This would mean that
September 10, 1985

we would end up litigating against ourselves under the Minister's proposal by withdrawing the 1970 reservation.
In conclusion, let me congratulate the Right Hon. Minister on his new-found interest in boundaries, the Polar 8 and accompanying declarations. I think they are very Canadian. Let me ask the Minister to move now on aboriginal title, complete boundary actions,-including a movement today, I hope, because the Americans no doubt will have listened, under COGLA which is very important in terms of law- submarine rights, economic development in the north and with caution in the environment so sensitive to change. It is the great desert of the north.
I heard great applause from that side of the House encouraging navigation, but we have to deal with Lancaster Sound and many other very serious and sensitive ecological matters first.
Finally, I ask the Right Hon. Minister to understand the fear of Canadians of connecting the North Warning System and the forward bases for F-18 interceptors to missile bases, star wars and the front line of Fortress America. It is a powerful image. The previous Hon. Member who spoke touched on the humiliation of the summer, but it is a matter of imagery about which Canadians are very frightened. Our North was penetrated this summer. With all the overlying factors, there is a real fear in the country about the whole issue.
In conclusion, let us somehow make the Arctic nuclear-free and fully sovereign from the psychological rape this summer by the penetration of the Polar Sea.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have in hand a petition signed by a hundred workers from Quebec who are asking that all retired employees keep their pension benefits and receive their unemployment insurance allowances without any deduction from their pension income.

The problem toward which this petition is directed affects workers across the country.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition from a number of Winnipeg residents who protest the move by the Government to deduct benefits from unemployment insurance benefits. It will have a detrimental impact upon family income and robs people who have worked a lifetime of the pension benefits
Order Paper Questions
which they have earned. The petitioners call upon the Government to reverse its intention in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present some petitions. One is from the Province of New Brunswick and it is signed by several residents of that province. The others are from Edson, Alberta; Prince George, British Columbia; and Scarborough, Ontario.
These petitioners ask the Government to change the particular provision of the Unemployment Insurance Act which would make pension income deductible from unemployment insurance.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-66, an Act respecting the reorganization of the Canada Development Corporation, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

I am advised that when the House rose at one o'clock there were five minutes remaining in the question and answer period. Is the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) rising to participate in the debate?
Yes.
Before recongizing the Hon. Member, may 1 indicate that according to Standing Order 19(4) the sitting of the House will be extended by 33 minutes.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise with regret to speak on this Bill to privatize the Canada Development Corporation because I think that the CDC, whether it is under the Conservatives or whether it was under the Liberals, in the period since its foundation some 15 years or 18 years ago represents a failed opportunity for Canadians. It represents a failed opportunity in terms of diversification of the Canadian economy, in terms of its original goals, and in terms of the possibility of creating a different model of the way an economic organization or corporation would work to serve the people of Canada, its owners, and to serve the workers, customers and suppliers who dealt with and worked for the various entities under the control of that corporation. It is a failed opportunity in terms of a kind of model which could have been created for our future development.
The Macdonald Commission report has just been brought down. Unfortunately it is retrograde; it looks backward rather than forward. It seems to be looking into a rear-view mirror in terms of its idea about the kind of corporate Canada we could have in the future.
It is regrettable because during its earlier stages the Macdonald Commission asked appropriate questions about what kind of future organization we could have in our economy to ensure that we were flexible and adaptable to change and to ensure that ordinary working people could feel that they were
September 10, 1985

a part of our economic society rather than feel that they were simply pawns, that they were exploited by society or that they had no say in the wayin which things were run.
The Canada Development Corporation has grown to a $4 billion or a $5 billion corporation in a few short years. It could have been a model by which working people could have in fact had a say in the future of the enterprise within which they were involved. The Liberal Government, which went down in defeat last year, did not see it that way. In fact, it successively loosened its grip on the CDC until it was almost not worth the bother to try to resuscitate it as an instrument of public policy. However, there was still a strong case to be made that the CDC as an instrument of public policy or as a public corporation could have shown how the public sector could in fact be different and still be efficient, profitable and all the other things which were put forward as its goals and objectives.
Under the Conservatives there simply was not a chance. I now have the honour to be the critic of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens). Once that Minister came to power, he was determined to proceed with privatization. In that goal he had the support of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and, I suppose, the tacit support of other Members of the Government. They did not stop to see whether there were some other alternatives. They did not stop to see what might be the consequences of letting this major portion of our economy go into private hands. They did not stop to ask themselves whether or not this really was in the best interests of Canadians. As far as the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion was concerned, it was a good thing if it was in the private sector and it was a bad thing if it was left in the public sector and therefore it had to go. One of the reasons offered by the Minister for this was that Crown corporations should be sold in the event that they were not fulfilling a public policy purpose. I think it can be argued that the Canada Development Corporation has ceased to fulfil a public policy purpose becuase it was being run as a private sector conglomerate corporation with next to no input as far as the public sector was concerned.
Through the years, the Canada Development Corporation did play somewhat of a public role. It made some investments in high tech early on. It Canadianized the Texas Gulf Mine in Timmins which is now known as the Kidd Creek Mine and brought it into Canadian hands. It has pioneered investments in the field of biotechnology. The Canada Development Corporation took over control of Connaught Laboratories and sought to modernize that particular institution which had belonged to the University of Toronto for many years. It sought to make it effective, efficient and competitive in order to allow it to continue to make a contribution to Canadian life as one of the only pharmaceutical companies in the country carrying out indigenous research and developing products here in Canada rather than simply importing patents from elsewhere.
The fact is that the CDC, in its early years, did seek to fulfil a public policy purpose but it lost its direction quite quickly. I
Canada Development Corporation cannot think of anything that it has done in the last few years which really indicates a particularly strong thrust. 1 think it epitomizes one of the problems of public ownership which has been endemic under both the Liberal and Conservative Governments which is that when there are governments that do not believe in public ownership and accountability and when there are governments that do not understand that public ownership should be something different from private ownership, then it fact Crown corporations will not be particularly effective. That has been the case with Canada Development Corporation.
What is happening now? As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) has said, the Government has finally announced its plans. On June 27, a day or two before the House rose for the summer, a Bill was put before the House by the Minister. There was a long summer recess and now the Bill is being rushed through the House by the Government. Did the Government at least have the grace to wait until the Bill was enacted before it acted as though it were law? The answer is no. Not only is the answer no, but quite specifically the share offering which was undertaken this summer in Toronto and on the Financial markets of Canada directly contravened the existing Canada Development Corporation Act and permitted a private-sector corporation, Noranda, to effectively take over 25 per cent control of the Canada Development Corporation despite the fact that the law currently reads that until this Act is amended if it is to be amended, no individual shareholders should have more than 3 per cent ownership of the Canada Development Corporation with the exception of the Government of Canada.
Noranda is effectively buying operating control of the Canada Development Corporation. I am not sure if that was intentional on the part of the Government. Did Mr. Zimmerman of Noranda meet with the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion in order to arrange all of this? Is the fix in so that the Kidd Creek Mine will be absorbed into the mining operations of Noranda and the rest of the Canada Development Corporation will be spun off to private sector shareholders? Will there be any limitations if Noranda decides to sell off Polysar, a corporation which has been a Crown corporation for some 40 years, into American hands so that the synthetic rubber activities will become a part of Goodyear, B. F. Goodrich or one of those companies? We do not know. We may find out during the course of the committee hearings but the fact is that we do not know.
Major elements of our economy are being privatized. If we ask what has happened when we find that companies have been shut down, that ownership has been spun off or that they have been bought piece by piece by foreign multinationals, we will be told by Ministers of the Crown that those are commercial activities over which they do not have any control.
Today in the House of Commons the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) gave us an example of something like that. Last March, she was involved in the bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank in which six commercial banks contributed $60 million to a rescue operation that we were assured would make the CCB a viable entity once again.

September 10, 1985
Canada Development Corporation
Shortly after that, those banks and other Canadian chartered banks proceeded to systematically bring their deposits in the CCB down to the lowest tolerable level. They brought their deposits down to a mere $5 million from $41 million in the course of a few short weeks. When the Minister was asked today if she did anything about that, if she knew about it and if she tried to stop it, she said that those were commercial activities and she had no power to stop them.
The Bill before us not only allows the Government to reduce to nothing its shareholdings in the Canada Development Corporation, it also effectively provides a blueprint for the destruction of the Canada Development Corporation. For one thing, its name can be changed without recourse to Parliament. The Canada Development Corporation can become Noranda (CDC) Incorporated or it can be changed to Uncle Sam Incorporated if the new owners or controllers think that that is a good idea. The company could easily be controlled by Noranda and by a couple of other shareholders who do not have to be Canadians because foreign share ownership is to be permitted up to 25 per cent and individual foreign multinationals will have the right to own up to 10 per cent of what is now known as the Canada Development Corporation.
Now there are controls on the CDC but once the corporation is in private hands, will there be anything to stop the CDC from continuing the program of divestment that it has taken over the course of the last couple of years? Last year I was contacted by a friend of mine who was very concerned about what was happening with Connaught Laboratories. CDC systematically puffed up the value of Connaugh in order to sell the shares on the private market. It boasts about that in its most recent annual report. It stripped assets from the pension fund in order to help bolster the company's cash reserves.
Connaught represents only a modest proportion of CDC's total assets. However, the same thing could be done with Kidd Creek. Kidd Creek could be sold off through a share exchange with Noranda. It could be done with Canterra, a corporation which accounts for 8 per cent or 9 per cent of the annual sales of the Canada Development Corporation. It could be done with Polysar or with Petrosar, companies which are both wholly owned by the CDC and which account for half of the value of its sales on an annual basis.
In a few months, we may well read in The Globe and Mail Report on Business that these corporations have been spun off in very much the same way as were portions of the CDC's ownership in Connaught Laboratories. In other words, this entire entity may simply disappear or it may turn into a totally different type of conglomerate, certainly one which would serve no functional purpose at all in terms of public policy. It would simply be a vehicle for making money, for providing jobs for corporate leaders and perhaps incidentally for helping to maintain a certain sector of the economy by contributing to the prosperity of Canadians, but only incidentally. I find that very disappointing.
It seems to me that a new Government which was elected on a mandate of change and which has revealed itself prepared on a number of occasions to rethink the shibboleths which it
brought into office when it was elected last September 4 might well have looked at the Canada Development Corporation not as a problem, not as a dog to be divested of in the manner of the Harvard Business School, but as an opportunity for Canadians.
I draw to the attention of Members of the Government Party the contrast between the development of the CDC on the one hand and la Caisse de depot and Placements de Quebec on the other. The Caisse de depot was established in 1966 or thereabouts as a vehicle for Quebec Government investments around the same time the Quebec Pension Plan was being established to parallel the Canada Pension Plan. It used funds which were invested in it from the Quebec Pension Plan. It was assured, therefore, that as an investment of public policy, it would have a continuing and growing source of capital which could be used for the diversification and expansion of the economy of the Province of Quebec. Since Quebecers were the contributors to the fund, it was quite natural that it was used as an instrument of public policy. Many corporations in manufacturing, textiles, steel and pulp and paper industries have now had major shareholdings acquired by the Caisse de depot. Canadian Pacific is now partially controlled by the Caisse de depot and in fact the Caisse de depot has become such a large operator in the financial markets of the country that the private sector is crying uncle and saying that it is suffering from unfair competition. The previous Liberal Government tried to pass a piece of legislation which would have clipped the wings of the Caisse de depot in order that it would not get too large. It is one of the curiosities of the private sector that when it feels that the heat is on it comes to the Government asking that the rules be changed in order to favour it. It does this when the going is getting a bit too competitive.
That is something which has been done by a pension fund in one province. The Caisse de depot has become a major actor in financial markets right across the country. The Canada Development Corporation could have done that as well. However, it was not done because the Liberal Government of the day, after an initial burst of enthusiasm, did not carry out what it intended to do when the idea of a Canada Development Corporation was dreamed up by Walter Gordon, when the nationalists within the Liberal Party-and there were a few in those days-saw it as an instrument of the Canadian economy, of an economy that would be owned and controlled by Canadians.
The CDC stopped its efforts to Canadianize our economy God knows how many years ago. It simply settled down into a corporate very much like any other. I had a look at the Board of Directors of the corporation which, even up until today, is something in the order of 87 per cent or 90 per cent controlled by the people of Canada, who are currently the shareholders until this Bill is passed, if it is passed, and until the tentative share issue made in the summer has been legitimized by Parliament. I looked to see how this public corporation had been made somehow different from any other conglomerate in the country. I wanted to see how it reflected the vast diversity
September 10, 1985

of our country and of our population. I have to say, with regret, that I could find no difference between this corporation and Power Corporation, CP Investments, or any other private sector corporation. Of the 20 people on the Board of Directors,
I found one representative of the Government of Canada. That is the Deputy Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. There were no other representatives of the people of Canada, despite the fact that we, as the people of Canada, hold 87 per cent or 90 per cent of the shares. There are two women on the Board of Directors-hardly bold leadership of a Government dedicated to showing that women should have a place of equality in the economic life of our country. In 20 years no government ever got around to appointing more than women to the Board of Directors.
It is common knowledge on Bay Street and St. James Street that the direction of the Canada Development Corporation has been very much in the hands of Anthony Hampson and the group around him and that they have successfully fought off overdue influence and participation from the chief shareholder. That chief shareholders, the Government of Canada, has simply sat back and taken it rather than saying that the Canada Development Corporation is different to ensure that it will be run in a manner which, in fact, is different.

Mr. Speaker, we in this Party are against this Bill to privatize the Canada Development Corporation. We intend to vote against this piece of legislation because we believe the Government missed a good opportunity when it decided to get rid of its shares in this corporation instead of seeking an efficient and novel way to use this group of companies, with assets of about $5 billion, to the benefit of all Canadians.
We have in this country an economic culture which readily lends itself to a mixed economy. We have Crown corporations such as Air Canada, Canadian National Railways and, until now, the Canada Development Corporation, Ontario has Ontario Hydro, Quebec has Hydro-Quebec, and practically all provinces have power companies in the public sector, telephone and transportation companies, marine companies, communications and satellite companies which belong to us as Canadians. A great many of those companies are healthy and quite profitable and they must remain under public ownership so that Canadians will have the necessary means and tools to control and direct their own economy and make sure that it is managed in the best interest of Canada as a whole. Unfortunately, notwithstanding the wide variety of public companies and Crown corporations existing in Canada, we have been unable to find the means to manage those corporations in a way that is significantly different from the way privately owned companies are managed. For instance we have failed to find ways to ensure the participation of workers, possibly those who buy from or sell to those companies. We have not really developed different ways that would enable those companies to operate much differently from privately owned companies.
Canada Development Corporation

That is a pity because it seems to me that we are different in this country. One of the reasons our economy differs from that of the United States is because of the fact that, essentially, the United States does not have public ownership. It does not have the ideology which believes in public ownership and, therefore, there is little or no public sector involvement in the economy of the United States.
I recall going to Minnesota some years ago and talking to the Secretary of Commerce there. I asked him what activities there were in the State in the public sector. After describing what we did in Ontario, where I was an MPP, he thought for a long time and said: "Well, I think that our sewers are publicly owned." That was all. That is a great pity because there is a role for the public sector.
We, in Parliament, responding to the people of-my time is up.

Questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper).

Mr. Speaker, the remarks of my colleague have given me reason for reflection. Can he elaborate on the potential damage to the Canadian economy with respect to eliminating the role of the public sector in the Canadian economy? Will he tell us just how much of a risk we are running in terms of our economic health by going on a privatization binge?

I would like to respond to the Hon. Member and give a specific example, which is Polysar. Over the last 40 years, Polysar has become a genuine success story and a Canadian multinational corporation. It was founded during the war to produce artificial and synthetic rubber because of the needs of wartime. It was maintained in public ownership since 1945. Now, for what amounts to a modest amount of revenues to the people of Canada, we are receiving about $200 million from the sale of all of the corporations in the conglomerate called the Canada Development Corporation. We are giving up control of Polysar. While the corporate shell, the Canada Development Corporation, is meant to stay in Canadian hands, there is nothing to stop CDC, under its new ownership, from selling off Polysar. This is a successful Canadian multinational which has operations in 40 or 50 countries around the world. There is nothing to stop the CDC from

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly to this Bill and to review why the Government is putting it forward for consideration at this time. It is part of our effort as a Government to rationalize the Crown corporations which we found in the portfolio when we assumed office. We have made efforts to privatize some, but the purpose of the Bill which we are discussing today is to remove four Crown corporations which serve no useful public purpose. Indeed, three of these Crown corporations are completely inactive and the fourth merely holds a piece of property for the Crown.
For the edification of the House, I intend to run through the intent behind the Bill as it deals with each of the four Crown corporations. The first is Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, Ltd. which was incorporated under the Dominion Companies Act in 1927 to provide a steamship service to the West Indies. The corporation has been inactive since 1958 when its fleet of ships was sold to Banco Cubana of Havana. In 1959 the corporate management was transferred to federal Government officials for the purpose of collecting the proceeds from the sale. An irrevocable letter of credit was issued through the Bank of America to cover the final principal payment which was not honoured due to the passing of the Cuban Assets Control Regulations by the Government of the United States on July 3, 1963. The sole purpose of maintaining the company is to collect the outstanding principal plus interest totalling perhaps $900,000 as of December 31, 1984. These funds are frozen today in the Bank of America in New York.
The Department of Finance, in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), is the registered holder of the share certificates. That Department and the Department of External Affairs are making efforts and representations, now that our relations with Washington have been improved, to secure the release of the frozen funds. If that approach does not succeed within a reasonable period of time, steps will be taken to ensure that the present obligation owing to Canadian National (West Indies) from the sale of its steamships would become an obligation enforceable by Her Majesty. This would necessitate a written agreement with the Bank of America that it would eventually reassign the payment to Her Majesty if Canadian National (West Indies) were dissolved. In any event, that will go forward if in fact this Bill is passed. We do not intend to dissolve the corporation formally until we are certain that the outstanding balance of approximately $1 million will be paid to the Crown.

September 10, 1985
Crown Corporations
The second Crown corporation to be dissolved is the Societa a Responsibilita Limitata Immobiliare San Sebastiano which was acquired by the Department of External Affairs as a means of purchasing, without tax penalties, the official residence of the Canadian Ambassador to the Holy See in Rome, Italy. This was a private Italian company whose sole asset was a residence. I might say that it was the subject of some discussion in one of the Auditor General's reports some time ago. Normally External Affairs purchases these residences directly on behalf of Her Majesty. What we are proposing now is to change the company into a limited partnership and subsequently to have the property donated to the Crown. We will then proceed to have approval of the acceptance of the gift by Her Majesty the Queen in right of Canada authorized by the Government of Italy pursuant to Article 10 of the Italian Civil Code. Officials are pursuing the ramifications and methods of doing that at the moment.
The third Crown corporation to be wound up is St. Anthony Fisheries Limited which was established in 1982 to reopen and operate but not own a dormant fish processing plant at St. Anthony, Newfoundland. It was agreed that the plant's owner, Fishery Products which, as the House will know, has now merged with Fishery Products International Limited, would market production during the 1982 season. This plant is now owned and operated by Fishery Products International Limited which is the combined entity set up in Newfoundland under the Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act.
Because FPIL has now taken over the operation of the St. Anthony plant, St. Anthony Fisheries is an inactive corporation. It continues to exist as a shell corporation in order to collect arrears from FPIL with respect to sales made on behalf of St. Anthony Fisheries by Fishery Products. The corporation will not be wound up until these arrears are collected.
When the corporate plan for St. Anthony Fisheries Limited was approved by the Treasury Board in March 1985, the Treasury Board requested that the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) settle the arrears of FPIL to St. Anthony Fisheries prior to or in conjunction with his next request for funds for FPIL. Action on this request is expected before the end of this curent calendar year.
The last Crown corporation with which we are dealing in this Bill is Uranium Canada, Ltd. which was created in 1971 pursuant to Appropriation Act No. 1, 1971, and the Atomic Energy Control Act with a mandate to purchase $29.5 million worth of uranium concentrates on behalf of the Crown from Denison Mines Ltd. over the period 1971 to 1975.
During the period 1971 to 1980, Uranium Canada sold or made loans of portions of the stockpile and returned some $114 million to the Crown. During this time, uranium prices increased and Canada's known reserves increased dramatically, primarily due to the discovery of large, rich deposits in Saskatchewan. Therefore, the need for a Canadian Government stockpile or government support of Canadian mines disappeared.
In May 1981, the Government transferred the ownership of the remaining stockpile having a book value of $96 million to Eldorado Nuclear Ltd. and directed the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to wind up Uranium Canada. However, the House will recall that the company was subsequently charged along with five other uranium companies with offences under the Combines Investigation Act. The matter was finally settled on December 15, 1983, when the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that Uranium Canada, as an agent of the Crown, was immune from the terms of the Combines Investigation Act.
Uranium Canada is now dormant, having no operations, no staff and assets totalling $9. The company's affairs are conducted on an as required basis by Public Service employees and its resource requirements are minimal. There being no further use for the corporation, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) is requesting the authority of Parliament to dissolve it.
These are the corporations which we are planning to dissolve at this time. I think they can best be described as loose ends. I would refer to one other Crown corporation which is not referred to in this Bill. For the edification of the House, there was a fifth Crown corporation, Mingan Associates, a corporation which it had been our intention to dissolve as well. It was the owner of some land in Quebec which the Government subsequently transferred to native people. speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending the current bankruptcy legislation to provide farmers and fishers with a pre-bankruptcy arbitration procedure which would provide them with, as a last resort, a court ordered settlement to be fully binding on all creditors and the farmer(s) or fisher(s) involved.
He said: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The motion I have before the House today is inspired by the terribly serious situation which we have in agriculture at this time. It is a situation which we have had for the past year or so with regard to the loss of farm equity, the loss of farms, and so on.
Hon. Members will note that the motion is dated April 1, 1985. It is so dated because it became apparent at that time, after an experiment which was carried out in Bruce County, which was a pilot project, that there really had to be legislation of this nature put before the House and adopted by Parliament in order to deal with bankruptcies in the farming sector. 1 would like to quote a couple of figures in that regard. Last October, we received a report which indicated that some 17 per cent of farmers were in serious financial difficulty. This

September 10, 1985
Bankruptcy Act
year, when that report was examined, some 18 months after the original study was carried out, the percentage of farmers in serious financial difficulty had risen to some 23 per cent. Farm asset values had dropped by 12 per cent from $116 billion to $102 billion, a massive loss of equity by farmers.
The discouraging part of the reports, which indicate the serious financial difficulty in our farming communities, were even more distressing because most of the farmers in difficulty were our youngest, our most productive and our most technologically advanced. Apart from that, the studies indicate that some 50 per cent of all the food produced in our country was produced by these young farmers who are in serious financial difficulty.
In the past weeks, the crisis has heightened. For instance, I have been told by representatives of the Farm Credit Corporation that in the first two months of this fiscal year there were 169 foreclosures by the Corporation. That is a rate of 87 per cent faster than in the previous year. That works out to 11 farms a week which are being taken over by the Farm Credit Corporation.
The Bruce County study indicated that the Farm Credit Corporation, because of its current rules and regulations, is not willing to write down any of the debt which it holds with young farmers. The procedure proposed in my motion would allow for this to take place.
In Bruce County, recently, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture passed a resolution suggesting that there be a declaration of a moratorium on farm foreclosures. This took place at a meeting in Chesley on August 29 which was attended by some 200 or 300 farmers who were calling on the Government to take action. The OFA will be considering that resolution further at its regular meeting on September 18.
Clearly, the situation is chaotic. There needs to be better procedures. I suppose we are more concerned because the Government has really taken no action to provide, in the Budget, for instance, a special write down procedure for lower interest rate loans. We have seen action by the new Ontario Liberal Government; but there has been no action taken by our Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
I have had contact as well with young farmers in the Maritimes who are calling for action in this regard, as is proposed in the motion. I have heard from farmers in western Canada. In July, I had an opportunity to visit some of the areas hit by drought in southern Saskatchewan. I met with dozens of farmers at a conference in Moose Jaw. At that time we saw the ravages of the massive reduction in farm values and the continuing low commodity prices.
We recently heard a call from the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool for a $500 million program to assist the grain growers of western Canada. We have all seen the clips on television news reports of farm families applying for welfare and many farmers desperate with thoughts of losing their farms.
The motion before the House today proposes that the Government get on with the legislation which was before the House in the previous Parliament under Bill C-17. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) on July 10 said that he would be bringing forward such legislation. Thus far we have not seen it.
I hope that when the Parliamentary Secretary speaks this afternoon he will be able to indicate that in fact the Government is not just stalling and that it will get on with such legislation. Clearly, there is a question in everyone's mind because the same press clippings indicated that the Minister was going to bring forward such legislation while the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) has indicated that he did not know anything about it. He was in charge of the legislation so it seems highly in doubt that the Government is actually moving on this. Perhaps the Minister is just talking because of the tremendous need for action, but maybe no action is forthcoming.
In Bill C-17 of the previous Parliament there was a provision for people facing serious financial difficulty in that they could apply to the bankruptcy court to make arrangements with respect to their debt. Amendments were proposed at that time with respect to arrangements which would have applied to bankruptcies of more than $1 million in that a similar provision would be available for fishermen and farmers. The procedure, as I understand it, is one in which the farmer facing serious financial difficulty and on the verge of bankruptcy can file a notice of intention to secure an arrangement from the bankruptcy court. This would prevent his creditors from moving in on him. It would allow a trustee, secured by the farmer or fisherman, to negotiate an agreement with the creditors. Where an agreement was arranged around the table for a write down of debt, it would allow for that agreement to be simply filed with the registrar of the court and it would become effective on the debts of the individual. Where there was no agreement, the farmer could apply to the judge of the court and if the judge agreed to establish an arrangement for writing down the debt, he could appoint an expert panel of qualified people to assist the court in reviewing the circumstances of the situation and make a recommendation to the court and the judge could accept or reject or modify the panel's recommendation. If there were no agreements reached or if an agreement was rejected by the judge, it still would not deprive the farmer or fisherman of their rights in that they could not be petitioned into bankruptcy. Therefore, it would protect the rights of the farmer or fisherman in that regard.
So often we see in bankruptcies too much money and property lost. Everyone loses. In fact, the Farm Credit Corporation has said that in every bankruptcy they see something like $90,000 to $100,000 lost regardless of the circumstances of the bankruptcy. This procedure which was originally proposed in Bill C-17 would allow an arrangement for agreements between creditors and farmers in serious financial difficulty and perhaps in many cases would allow them to continue on in business while at the same time writing off substantial debts instead of not allowing them to continue in business.
My concern would be that this motion pass tonight to indicate the will of the House to support it and to indicate to
September 10, 1985

the Government to get on with it and bring in such legislation at any early date. 1 wish Government had adopted the recommendation of the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs which recommended a massive program of assistance to those farmers who are facing serious financial difficulty. However, Government did not do that and it will have to live with the political consequences of not taking action like the Ontario Government and other provincial governments.
I think there is a place for such legislation as is proposed in this motion. Clearly it seems like the Government has been procrastinating. The legislation was before the Committee 15 months ago. They have gone through the reports of the FCC indicating these serious financial difficulties. They have gone through a moratorium on foreclosures and they have studied the Bruce Country pilot project. There is apparently no money forthcoming from the Government in the Budget to deal with these serious financial difficulties. Now is the time for the Government to indicate that it is prepared to bring in this modest action which would help a certain number of farmers. The Minister indicated on July 10 he wants to do that.
We are waiting on so many things. We are waiting on the tripartite red meat decision by the Minister. We were disappointed there was no money in the Budget for the financial debt crisis. We are waiting on a dairy policy. We are waiting on aid for the western drought assistance program. We just hope that the Minister will get on with at least this legislation in order to bring it into the House at any early date because the situation in the West is desperate. It is going to become apparent with the rallies and marches which will take place this fall by groups like the Ontario Federation of Agriculture and other agricultural groups. They are desperate for help, especially those farmers in the grains and red meat industries because of the economics and climatic circumstances in other parts of the country.
I hope that the Government will not talk out this motion but allow it to pass. The support of the House has already been indicated. The Minister has already promised to introduce this legislation at an early time in this session.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   BANKRUPTCY ACT SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING PRE-BANKRUPTCY ARBITRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise in support of the motion before us today which calls upon the Government to amend the current bankruptcy legislation to provide farmers and fishermen with a pre-bankruptcy arbitration procedure, which would in turn provide as a last resort a court ordered settlement to be fully binding on all parties concerned. This proposal has been before the House for some time. As you will be aware, Mr. Speaker, it involves the Bankruptcy Act but it has a great effect on farmers. Farmers, as well as parliamentarians on this side of the House, are very patient people. We have waited a long time for a solution to the problems that changes to the Bank Act created for farmers some 15 or 18 years ago. We thought that Bill C-17 in the previous Parliament would redress the situation. As you know, we went into an election before that Bill proceeded through the House and we have waited over a year for it to be reintroduced. I am not sure what the problems in this respect have been, but when you go back and read the speeches in the last Parliament, particulary those by the Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) and the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), who is now chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, it appeared that we had at least achieved agreement on the question of how farmer and fishermen bankruptcies should be dealt with.
I pointed out that the problem seems to have arisen with changes to the Bank Act. That seems to be an oblique way of attacking the question, but in reality the bankruptcy legislation we have worked under has been pretty much the same since 1919. There were some minor amendments in 1949, but there were no real changes to the way a bankruptcy is proceeded with. Why, then, have there been problems in the intervening years? I submit it is because the Bank Act has resulted in some radical changes in the way security for loans to farmers and fishermen is handled. Under the old Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, lending institutions could provide a loan to a farmer or a fisherman under the following conditions. The borrower would have to put up 25 per cent of the cost of a new piece of equipment and the balance would be financed by the lending institution. The terms of the loan were very clear. The interest rate was fixed, usually at 5 per cent, sometimes 6 per cent. The term of repayment was made quite clear, from three to five years in most cases. The bank took security only on the equipment being purchased. If it was a fishing boat or a new tractor, that was the security. The Government of Canada insured the loans so that there were no untoward losses under this program.
Under that system the old Bankruptcy Act worked fairly well. Then we had changes to the Bank Act. The first change was in the late 1960s. Section 88 was added and the terms of the loans were changed quite dramatically. Instead of taking as security only the equipment being purchased, it was extended to the grain, livestock and machinery; in short, all of the movable inventory the borrower had on his farm or in his business. That was a substantial change in the amount of security required for a loan. Fortunately, the bank rate stayed the way it was written up in the original loan and the terms for repayment were spelled out quite clearly. However, when the Bank Act changed in 1980 or 1981, Section 178 dealt with these types of loans. Under that section we still offer all of our movable goods as security. As well, the interest rate changes whenever the bank decides it should and the loan is on call. It is no longer repayable over three to five years but is due any time the lending institution decides to call it.
Under those circumstances the old Bankruptcy Act is no longer adequate. Previous Governments have recognized that. The Liberal Governments of the 1970s, the short-lived Clark Government, and the last Liberal Government all attempted to change the Bankruptcy Act, but none of them succeeded in getting a new Act through the House. Just before the summer recess the then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) succeeded in achieving a consensus of the three Parties which would have treated farmers and fishermen in the same way as bankrupts of $1 million or more would be treated. The farmer or fisherman would have had the right to appear before a tribunal which would have examined all of the circumstances of the proposed bankruptcy and decided whether that farmer or fisherman had to go through the bankruptcy procedure or whether the lender should grant further time for payments to be made, or even go so far as to reduce the amount of the payments. That is quite a dramatic change from the way in which farmers and fishermen are treated under the present legislation.
Under the current Bank Act the rights of the lender have been over-extended and the borrower does not retain the protection which existed prior to the upsetting of the careful balance that had been struck between the old Bankruptcy Act and the old Bank Act. As the Bank Act changes there is
September 10, 1985

obvious need for changes to the Bankruptcy Act to recognize that new circumstance. We must ensure that the borrower has some rights in the arbitration between borrower and lender. That does not exist in the current Bankruptcy Act or in the current Bank Act. Nearly all of the rights and privileges lie with the lending institution and the borrower is very much at the mercy of that lending institution.
It is absolutely vital to farmers and fishermen in this country that there be immediate changes to the bankruptcy provisions of the Bankruptcy Act. There seemed to be universal agreement in the last session of Parliament and I had hoped that there would have been a new attempt to introduce a new version of the previous Bill C-17. We were near the end of a long road of attempting to make major amendments to the bankruptcy laws of this country. I urge the Government to reinitiate that process and reintroduce Bill C-17 which was agreed to just before the last session of Parliament adjourned.
We waited and watched as the current Government went through the Bruce County experiment. We hoped that something would develop from that which would be of use to farmers and could be adapted to fishermen. It appears that we waited in vain. It is now time to introduce a new version of the old Bill C-17 which will deal fairly and adequately with bankruptcy problems which have arisen due to changes in the Bank Act as they affect farmers and fishermen. I am sure that the Government is aware of the major financial problems that face farmers and fishermen in particular and I would urge it to reintroduce the necessary legislation as quickly as possible in order that farmers and fishermen can again be fairly dealt with in the process of bankruptcy.
