He said that farm producers were being offered cute little programs, but that agriculture did not need cute little programs. Farmers needed help in dealing with their problems and concerns. To my mind, the few announcements that were repeated earlier by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture were just so many cute little programs that have made farmers feel very disappointed and
Bankruptcy Act
also made them very anxious about the future, about whether they will be able to make a living on those operations in which they have invested tens of thousands of dollars.
We are still waiting for the long-term dairy policy that was promised with a great deal of fanfare and is now being promised again. We are still waiting for the $13 million and for what the Government is going to do with Bill C-25, the legislation on agricultural stabilization. In other words, there is a lot of anxiety, insecurity and trauma. There are many, many producers in Quebec, like everywhere else in Canada, who are worried about the future and are wondering whether this year it will be their turn to be hit by bankruptcy. 1 think they have every reason to be worried.
This brings me to the motion presented by my hon. colleague from Algoma which, in the circumstances, appears to be a very interesting and fascinating proposal, I am surprised the Government did not itself initiate the appropriate corrective action.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, when we are talking about the agro-food sector, I think every self-respecting society tends to have, or should have, self-sufficiency in the agro-food sector as its objective. I feel this is a generally recognized principle and a goal we all want to achieve.
Mr. Speaker, in my view, this presupposes that the Government is prepared to help and support those who are helping to feed the country.
Agriculture over the last decades has enjoyed, and rightly so, a number of privileges in terms for instance of subsidies, loans, special treatment as a vital industry in our society, and in fact it needs that support for a good many reasons. Here we have an industry that is dependent on nature. It is dependent on markets. And, finally, when things go wrong, it is not necessarily because of mismanagement or neglect. In many cases it is the result of a number of factors beyond the control of producers.
Mr. Speaker, ever since I entered politics I have always been surprised to see from time to time, and increasingly over a number of years unfortunately, that many farm operations are forced into bankruptcy. When I see a family farm that has been in operation for years being liquidated, the question that comes to my mind is: Who benefits? The corporation more often than not takes over the assets; these assets are left to themselves and deteriorate over the years. There are virtually no offers to purchase in 1985, because of the market situation, for it is extremely difficult to earn one's living on a farm. Those assets deteriorate to such an extent that they become useless at some point. And when we consider the situation in the months that follow the bankruptcy, we realize that finally everybody has lost. The family who lived from the industry, who used to produce, to contribute to the regional, provincial and national economy, who made an honest living on the farm simply lose all that, after having worked on it as a family, to a truly unbelievable extent. Who benefits? In what way? The

September 10, 1985
Bankruptcy Act
answer is, no one benefits whatsoever. The community loses a lot of money, the bank loses, because there are less and less potential purchasers for that kind of assets.
And I say: Why not? Knowing that with the current legislation, we are going to lose a lot of money anyway. Why not, through regulations or legislation of sort, try and find a way to allow these families or these farmers to keep their farms and facilities and continue in the agricultural industry.
A major problem within the farm community is who will take over the farms. As my honourable friend mentioned a while ago, our youngest, most productive and technologically advanced farmers are those who are facing the most serious financial difficulties. These same young farmers who are willing to work hard and who are responsible for most of the food produced in our country are unable to meet their financial commitments because of high interest rates, natural disasters, the market uncertainties and are on the verge of bankruptcy.
If we had means or mechanism to keep these young farmers on the farm, in my view they could continue to perform and contribute very significantly, because I believe the continued success of our agricultural community is fundamental and vital to the economic well-being of their areas and the whole of Canada.
To my mind, the interesting aspect of a measure such as this one, Mr. Speaker, is that the Government keeps telling us day in and day out: Listen, our financial situation is so precarious that the Government simply cannot make new expenditures. We cannot secure the funds required to implement this or that measure. Well now, this is one measure which does not require any kind of funding. It is a measure which can be implemented without any investment whatsoever. As I see it, it is strictly a matter of political will implying that we have faith in our young farmers, that we have faith in men and women who are faced with problems and who, as I said, are in no way responsible for the current financial woes. It seems to me that, if not as a Government, at least as a society we might help those who have been forced to live with such problems, and that would not be tantamount to giving them a chance since nobody would stand to lose anything at all. It seems to me we might actively and openly support any measure to improve the agricultural food sector, an initiative which would surely boost productivity and benefit the agricultural community as a whole.
So I quite sincerely hope that, if we have so much faith in our agricultural food industry, if we are ready to support it, if we are quite willing to make a special effort, I sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, that the initiative of my colleague will be approved and supported to that it will lead to concrete measures at the earliest opportunity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to participate in this debate on the proposal by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). 1 know that he is very serious about that matter and has given it much consideration.
However, it should be pointed out that one reason why we are debating a motion concerning bankruptcy today is that the previous Government simply did not take agriculture very seriously. Rather than debating the future of agriculture we are debating how to cure some of the ills of the past.
The Hon. Member for Algoma would indicate that farm bankruptcies only started a year ago last September 4. However, farm bankruptcies have been increasing since the late 1970s and one reason for that is the unreasonable interest rates which young farmers have had to pay as a result of mismanagement by the previous Government. They have had to pay the highest interest rates in the history of Canada.
They were also told to borrow, plant large amounts of crops and modernize their equipment. They were told that what they would grow would be sold by the Government. Unfortunately, those words ring rather hollow today. Those farmers are now facing bankruptcy.
The Hon. Member mentioned a program which is now in effect in Ontario. We know that that program is simply an election gimmick. The farmers will receive a small amount of money now but will lose it after the next election. I do not believe that Ontario farmers want election gimmicks to solve their problems.
Many farmers owe hundreds of thousands of dollars but their equity is not enough to cover their debts. Today we are discussing how to save them from bankruptcy. One of the first steps taken by our Minister last fall was to impose moratorium on farm bankruptcies. This was followed by an interest rate adjustment program to lower those high interest rates imposed on farmers by the previous Government.
As was mentioned, the Government also set up a pilot program in Grey-Bruce to determine whether something could be done to help those farmers in cases of arbitration. Studies showed that farmers face very grave problems, especially those involved in the beef business. Those of us who represent rural areas realize how tragic it is that a farm that began generations before must now go on the auction block because of bankruptcy.
I would like to go over some of the figures and bring this House up to date on the present situation regarding the Farm Credit Corporation. There are serious financial difficulties in agriculture today. A Farm Credit Corporation survey published last year, and a more recent update, suggests that some 23 per cent of farmers are experiencing financial difficulty.
The difficulties in the farm sector are well reflected in the FCC lending. In the 1984-85 fiscal year, the demands for loans dropped by 59 per cent from a record level the year
September 10, 1985

before. This year the level of lending is likely to be even lower, which reflects just how bad the farm economy is.
Other evidence of difficulties can be found in the arrears figures for the Farm Credit Corporation. On August 1, about 17,000 or 22 per cent of Farm Credit accounts were in arrears. This is a sign of the difficulties farmers are facing. It is a reflection of the fact that the FCC's role is to provide credit to beginning farmers unable to obtain financing from commercial sources. This means that FCC's borrowers represent the riskiest part of the agricultural credit market.
Although it is not possible to save every farming operation, the Corporation is sensitive to the cyclical nature of agriculture. Thus it has a compassionate policy with respect to those in arrears. The Corporation has been known to carry some accounts in arrears for several years, something that few other creditors would be willing to do. This policy is meant to give borrowers time to explore every available option to keep them in business. Unfortunately, in some cases there are few options and a farmer has little choice but to close down.
At the moment, over 6,000 loans are under recovery action. A total of 42 FCC borrowers filed for bankruptcy between April 1 and July 31, 1985. During the 1984-85 fiscal year, 96 FCC borrowers declared bankruptcy. The year before there were 121. Often, of course, it is not the FCC that forces the farmer to declare bankruptcy, but other creditors. However, the Corporation's employees are working closely with farmers to try to help them organize their finances to cope with today's difficulties in which they find themselves. Currently over 3,000 of the the Corporation's borrowers are receiving formal financial counselling through the Corporation's advisory services program.
The legacy of a large federal deficit has given this Government very little room to manoeuvre to respond to these difficulties. Despite this, I believe that our Government has taken a number of positive steps to solve the credit problems of agriculture.
Soon after taking office, the Government responded by suspending the Farm Credit Corporation recovery actions for two months to give the Government and the FCC's borrowers breathing space in which to look for solutions for farm financial problems. Subsequently, the mandate of the FCC appeal board was extended to include the review of FCC foreclosure cases. These boards are made up of practising, experienced farmers who can offer an impartial, third-party analysis of each borrower's situation. From January 15 to July 31, 1985, about 65 cases have been heard by the appeal boards. In 14 cases, alternatives to foreclosure were recommended and FCC concurred. In 49 cases, the appeal boards upheld the FCC decision. Decisions are pending in the remaining two cases.
During the past year, the over-all trend in interest rates has been downward. This has been of tremendous benefit to the agricultural sector. Farm Crown Credit corporation charges 11 Vi per cent on its loans with five year interest rate terms and 11.5 per cent on its shared risk mortgage program. While we would like interest rates to fall even lower, these are, in fact, the lowest rates charged by the Corporation since 1979.
Bankruptcy Act
In 1981-82, interest rates had reached record levels. Some FCC borrowers were locked into long-term mortgages at interest rates as high as 16.75 per cent. We know this is when many of our young farmers first got into difficulty. To assist these borrowers, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), announced earlier this year that borrowers who took out loans in 1981 and 1982 at rates above 14 per cent would be helped by an interest rate reduction program.
Over 5,400 FCC borrowers accepted the conversion of their mortgages to a five year term at 12.75 per cent. This important assistance was provided through foregone revenue to the Government of Canada. The FCC was allowed to use about $600 million of its 1984-85 borrowing authority to refinance its outstanding high interest rate loans at a lower rate. Over five years, this will provide a benefit of approximately $80 million to the borrowers who took part in this program.
In April, 1984, the FCC expanded its credit options to farmers. It began to offer five, ten and 20 year fixed interest terms. This gave borrowers a greater range of choices compared to the single 10 year term offered previously. More choice meant more flexible financial planning.
Since then, another option, a 15 year term, has been added. As well, in April, 1985, the new FCC shared risk mortgage was introduced. This innovative mortgage is meant to respond to the economic forces affecting today's farmer.
In the 1980s, one of the problems that farmers faced was not just high interest rates, but the fact that interest rates fluctuated greatly. This increased the risk to farmers and made financial planning more difficult. At the same time, fixed interest rate loans taken out at a time when rates were high offered farmers little chance to benefit when rates fell.
The shared risk mortgage program offers protection against interest rate volatility. This unique mortgage offers security against increasing rates while also allowing borrowers to take advantage of decreases. The risk of annual interest rate changes are shared between borrower and lender. Moreover, a ceiling of 2.5 per cent is placed on increases.
Since its introduction, 190 or 17 per cent of FCC borrowers have opted for the shared risk mortgage. It is a realistic and innovative lending program. Farmers appreciate this act taken by the Government.
However, the Government's quest for solutions to the difficult financial problems of agriculture have not stopped with these initiatives. FCC officials are researching new programs. For example, a form of indexed loan is being examined.
The federal Government is very conscious of and deeply concerned with the problems facing farmers. In July, the Minister of Agriculture announced plans for an in-depth review of the role and mandate of the Farm Credit Corporation. The Minister invited anyone to submit ideas on the subject of the federal Government's role in the field of farm credit.
Farm Credit Corporation officials have been consulting with farmers, commercial and public sector lenders, provincial Governments, commodity groups and university researchers. A

diverse range of opinion has been offered, often reflecting common concerns about the level of interest rates and the need to help beginning farmers. The results of this consultation process are being compiled and will be ready in the near future.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that this points out just some of the actions our Government has taken to try to help farmers who have found themselves in great financial difficulty, and of course, we will continue to do so.

subtopic: APARTHEID-SOUTH AFRICA-REQUEST FOR ECONOMIC SANCTIONS. (B) REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE ACTION

speechtext:
Hon. Warran Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, on April 15, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) whether, considering the escalation of violence in South Africa, he was then ready to implement economic sanctions and a mandatory program with respect to Canadians doing business in South Africa. 1 also asked whether he would consult with the Opposition
September 10, 1985

Parties in order to develop a united national position with respect to South Africa.
In answering my question, the Minister replied that a review of this policy was under way at that time and that he would consult with the Opposition Parties. On the other hand, he was not ready at that time to announce any new policy. To his credit the Minister, through his Parliamentary Secretary, convened a meeting of representatives of all Parties. I attended on behalf of the Liberal Party; there was also a representative of the New Democratic Party. We met three times in an attempt to develop an all-Party position with respect to South Africa. Our purpose was to explore the possibility of developing a position on apartheid which would have all-Party support and would result in a unanimous resolution in the House of Commons.
At those meetings, I had proposed that the Government consider the following approaches: first, that he ban all new investment in South Africa; second, that there be a program of disinvestment; third, that there be no bank loans allowed to South Africa; fourth, that we stop Krugerrand sales in Canada; fifth, that we stop the landings of South African airlines in this country; sixth, that we completely boycott sports, cultural and scientific exchanges; seventh, that we have a mandatory code of conduct for Canadians doing business in South Africa; eighth, a full arms embargo; and ninth, a full energy embargo. I pointed out that many of these measures were already implemented or were in the process of being implemented in other countries; as a matter of fact, there are 22 Bills going through the American Congress this year in an attempt to implement all or several of those measures to which I have referred. The most important of those Bills are House of Representatives Bill 1460 and Senate Bill 635. As well, the Swedish Parliament passed a law banning all new investment in South Africa.
Unfortunately, it was not possible for Parliament to pass an all-Party resolution during the last week of the Session due to the many other matters which preoccupied Parliament. As a result, the Minister made a statement on his own behalf on July 6, a week after Parliament adjourned. While that statement of new policy was a step in the right direction and imposed more severe restrictions on South Africa with respect to Canada, it was not enough. The code of conduct is still a voluntary code. It is not mandatory and, stricktly speaking, there were no economic sanctions imposed against South Africa although there were measures to discourage Canadian trade with South Africa.
Since July, the situation in South Africa has deteriorated. There are now emergency measures in place in that country. Violence is escalating and deaths are reported each day, particularly in the black townships. Arrests of political leaders who are working for the good of the black African people are occuring.
Yesterday the President of the United States introduced some measures to deal with the South African situation. These
Adjournment Debate
measures go beyond those that have existed in the past against South Africa and go beyond those which were announced by Canada. However, they do not go as far as measures already voted on in the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives. They are not even acceptable to the moderates in South Africa.
I understand that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will make a statement later this week, perhaps tomorrow. I would urge him to go at least as far as the American Congressional Bills to which I have referred and at least as far as the Swedish Parliament. In the past, the Minister has rejected sanctions because he felt that they would destroy communications with the Government of South Africa and that they might hurt the blacks. That might have been a reasonable position at one time but it has been tried for several years and has not worked. It is time for something new.
In conclusion, I would say to the Government and the Parliamentary Secretary who is present that we have reached the point of no return. Everyone agrees that apartheid is wrong, injust, cruel and immoral. It is time to play hard ball with South Africa. We await the Minister's statement later this week. If it is a tough statement, I can assure the Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister that the Government will have the support of this Party and that we will be behind him 100 per cent in imposing tough measures on South Africa.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Kilgour (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subtopic: APARTHEID-SOUTH AFRICA-REQUEST FOR ECONOMIC SANCTIONS. (B) REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, through you, 1 hear my hon. friend loud and clear. We are discussing here today a tragedy which touches Canadians in their hearts. The revulsion felt by Canadians toward apartheid and indeed toward all forms of racial discrimination is very clear. Apartheid shrieks against everything that our multicultural society stands for.
The South African Government would have us believe that it is engaged in substantive reform. No one denies that blacks there have made economic and social progress in recent years. However, the fact remains that there are more than 300 apartheid laws still on the books which dictate where blacks must live, where their families must live, where they may work, where they may own land and where they may open and run a business. These laws deprive three-quarters of the population of basic civil rights, citizenship and the franchise.
It is not by incremental, piecemeal reform aimed at diluting such a system gradually that peace and elemental justice will come to South Africa. On this side of the House, we believe that something more basic is required from the present white minority Government. It is the heart of the system itself, not the tattered edges, which must be removed.
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, who is a white in South Africa? According to the law of the land, and I quote, it means:
-a person who (a) in appearance obviously is a white person and who is not generally accepted as a coloured person or (b) is generally accepted as a white person and who is not in appearance obviously not a white person.

September 10, 1985
Adjournment Debate
In deciding whether any person is in appearance obviously a white person or not a white person, within the definition of white person, his, and I quote again, "habits, education and speech and deportment and demeanor . . . shall be taken into account".
How can reasonable people anywhere accept this in the 1980s at the close of the 20th century? Who can blame the black population for their rising anger and frustration? Their plight is one which moves us; their struggle is one which we must share.
The situation in South Africa calls out for vigorous action. The Government of Canada has already acted in the right direction. In fact, Canada was the first major western country to take concrete steps, as announced on July 6-you are indicating that my time is up, Mr. Speaker.
Further measures are by no means ruled out at all. We will be working closely with our Commonwealth partners in the coming weeks on the run-up to the Heads of Government Meeting in Nassau next month. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), as my hon. friend pointed out, will be making a statement shortly on the matter.
Speaking personally, I am delighted that the Hon. Member has indicated for his Party that they will support us if we make a strong statement.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-RETENTION OF WINNIPEG AS REGIONAL HEADQUARTERS. (B) GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-RETENTION OF WINNIPEG AS REGIONAL HEADQUARTERS. (B) GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intention today is to follow up a concern which I first raised in a public way back in April, and one which I raised in the House on May 2 with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazan-kowski) concerning the consequences of the CNR appointing a Senior Vice-President for Western Canada to be located in Edmonton.
On May 2 I rose in the House and asked the Minister of Transport a question pertaining to that appointment because I was concerned that the CNR might be planning to revive a plan which it had in place a couple of years ago to amalgamate the Prairie Region, headquartered in Winnipeg, and the Mountain Region, headquartered in Edmonton, into one single region, the Western Canada Region, headquartered in Edmonton. I asked the Minister of Transport for assurances that that was not the case and that that action would not be carried out. The Minister of Transport said, and you can check the record, Mr. Speaker, "Yes, Mr. Speaker, I can give the Hon. Member those assurances".
Subsequent to those assurances it became clear to me through documents which I received from various people who worked at the railway, and from documents which others such as the MLA for Transcona, Mr. Wildon Parasiuk, received, that this type of amalgamation and consolidation of the two regions was going on and that Winnipeg stood to lose its position as a regional headquarters of the CNR.
It took a long time for those of us who knew this was happening to get the message across to those in Winnipeg who did not want to believe that it was actually happening. We knew that this was happening. On a number of occasions we released documentation to that effect. At one point 1 wrote to the Minister of Transport providing him with a document which came from the office of the senior vice-president. This document talked about the amalgamation of the Prairie and Mountain Regions. Yet when I received the Minister's answer after some time it simply referred me to a statement that Dr. LeClair had made in which he indicated that the CN had no plans to do this. Subsequently he had to come to Winnipeg and say that they had reversed their plans to do this. He apologized to the people of Winnipeg for the anxiety caused by the CNR through this move and said that it was now all cancelled, that it would never surface again and that the 10 appointments which had been made, and which constituted transfers of senior positions from Winnipeg to Edmonton, were cancelled. Those of us, Mr. Speaker, who were on to this move on the part of the CNR from the very beginning were very pleased to hear Mr. LeClair, as the chairman of the board of the Canadian National and chief executive officer for that company, say that this was now stopped and that it would not surface again.
But what 1 am concerned about is that over the coming few weeks we need to know whether or not the positions which were created in Edmonton called manager, Western Canada, have actually been abolished and whether or not the positions which were formerly abolished in Winnipeg have been recreated, because it will not be enough, Mr. Speaker, to simply cancel those appointments which constitute an actual transfer of certain people from Winnipeg to Edmonton. What we want to know is that the reorganization which caused those transfers to be made in the first place is actually cancelled. Otherwise, we will have only achieved a partial victory which will not in the long run protect Winnipeg from the kind of erosion of its status as a transportation centre. Therefore, I hope it will become clear to me and others who are concerned about this matter, Mr. Speaker, in the coming days and weeks that these new positions which were created in Edmonton and filled by people in Winnipeg-some of whom no longer have a job in Winnipeg because their old job as the senior regional person has been abolished-will in fact be abolished.
I am also concerned, Mr. Speaker, with the over-all attitude of the Government towards the transportation sector in Manitoba. There are a series of federal-provincial agreements with respect to building up the transportation sector in Manitoba which came about as a result of negotiations between the Province of Manitoba and the federal Government prior to the last election. One that I am particularly concerned about, for instance, has to do with agreements pertaining to the future of the Port of Churchill and a program for the rehabilitation of rolling stock, in this case, boxcars, which would serve the Port of Churchill. This is a program which has been agreed to and has been on the books for a long time now
September 10, 1985

but it seems to have a great deal of difficulty actually happening. It is of crucial importance to railway carmen in my riding who came back to work this week after a two-month lay-off, an extended shutdown, and were hoping that they would not be facing another lay-off in the very near future.
I am hoping that whoever is speaking for the Government-
I see the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) here, who perhaps will be responding on behalf of the Government-can indicate to us whether or not those federal-provincial agreements are now to be honoured and whether or not they have assurances from the CNR now that those positions which were created in Edmonton as part of the new western region have in fact been abolished and the senior positions which were abolished in Winnipeg have in fact now been reinstated. That is what we need to know, Mr. Speaker.

Winnipeg, Manitoba, is and will remain one of CN's greatest areas of activity. Over 7,000 CN employees work in Manitoba, representing more than one-third of the CN workforce in western Canada. board or the board of directors itself. That is why 1 called for his dismissal. That is out and out insubordination. Dr. LeClair did not say that the decision had been reversed. Contrary to statements made by the Hon. subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-REQUEST FOR FUNDING FOR REAL WOMEN ORGANIZATION
STATUS OF WOMEN-REQUEST FOR FUNDING FOR REAL WOMEN ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to take this opportunity to speak on behalf of the REAL Women organization. This group was formed in Toronto in 1983 by professional women and homemakers who joined together with 20,000 members from all across Canada. Their objective is to secure for all women a meaningful, equal and progressive role in the 1980s, an objective broadly embraced by the Government in freeing women from the effects of discrimination over the years.
REAL Women, although desiring equal opportunity for women in the workforce, as well stresses the importance of the family unit and the role of women as mothers and homemakers. Having witnessed the drastic changes that have altered our society in the last 20 years, the supporters of REAL Women have come forth with a very important point.
Throughout history the family has been the building block of our society and it is becoming increasingly obvious that the fragmentation of the family leads to a poorly functioning society and widespread social disorders are seldom unaccompanied by weakening family bonds. Alienation and delinquen-

September 10, 1985
Adjournment Debate
cy are most often the result of broken homes, in whatever circumstance.
REAL Women is a group that is sensitive to these dangers and they make this awareness a constant companion in their efforts to secure wider opportunities for women in society. In other words, Mr. Speaker, their agenda has been conceived to offer the greatest possible hope for progress for women while maintaining the family as a basis of Canadian society.
To date there has been a reluctance on the part of the Government to fund REAL Women, even though many other women's groups do receive such funding. I believe that if the Government is going to fund some women's groups, such as the National Action Committee for the Status of Women, it certainly should be funding another legitimate point of view like that of the REAL Women's organization. I strongly believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is not for a group of bureaucrats in the Ministry left over from the previous administration to decide which values best represent the interests of the women of Canada. REAL Women is a rapidly growing organization representing a view which I believe is widely held by a majority of Canadian women.
Many Members of the House have indicated to me their support for the approach taken by REAL Women. Also, thousands of women across Canada have shown their support through their membership and activism. The ideas put forth by this group represent a positive way for Canadian society to undergo important changes.
I have taken the opportunity of consulting with the new Minister, the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Bouchard), who has given me assurances that he will be looking into this situation and rendering a decision. I look forward to that news.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Landry (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-REQUEST FOR FUNDING FOR REAL WOMEN ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by thanking the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Jepson) for the interest he has shown in women's rights, thus demonstrating that all Progressive Conservative Members, irrespective of their sex, are concerned about the status of women.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to describe the role and the mandate of the Women's Program of the Department of the Secretary of State and explain why the Department decided against funding for REAL Women of Canada.
In 1973, a women's program was created at the Department to implement one of the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. Recognizing the important role played by women's voluntary associations in women's struggle for equal rights with men, the Commission recommended that the Government provide funding to encourage these associations to pursue their efforts, and also provide funding for other voluntary associations working in fields of particular concern to women.
The Women's Program is funding a broad range of women's groups across the country and in a broad cross-section of society to help them improve significantly the status of women in Canada.
The program tries to fund groups which through their activities are trying to make a positive contribution to the status of women, which are representative of the female population and whose work will benefit all Canadian women.
Although the work of women in the home constitutes an important contribution to society, the fact remains that in its efforts to improve the status of women-which were specifically referred to in the Throne Speech-the Government is not necessarily trying to promote a particular prototype of the family. This particular goals of REAL Women is not one of the objectives of the Women's Program, which tends to fund groups that see it as their task to explore the entire range of options women have in their struggle to achieve full equality.
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that women's rights groups have been working constantly to obtain recognition of the non-remunerated work done by women in the home. For instance, a number of organizations such as the National Action Committee on the Status of Women have been promoting for many years the concept of providing a pension for women in the home.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I can inform the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Jepson), as in fact he himself said earlier, that the Secretary of State who is responsible for the Women's Program intends to review and analyze all programs under his jurisdiction as part of a comprehensive study of his new duties.
